title: Planar Vectors, the Dot Product, Orthogonality, and Projections
subtitle: Displacement vectors in Q^2, algebraic and geometric dot products, perpendicularity u . v = 0, and scalar projections.
challenge: How does a simple sum of two products, u_1 v_1 + u_2 v_2, automatically know the angle between two vectors u and v in the plane—and why does it equal zero if and only if the vectors meet at a 90-degree right angle?
predictionPrompt: Find the exact rational value of k such that the planar vectors u = <4, 6> and v = <3, k> are orthogonal (perpendicular).
formalDefinition: For planar vectors u = <u_1, u_2> and v = <v_1, v_2>, the Euclidean norm is ||v|| = sqrt(v_1^2 + v_2^2) and the scalar dot product is u . v = u_1 v_1 + u_2 v_2. Applying the Pythagorean theorem (or Law of Cosines) to the triangle with sides u, v, and u - v proves the geometric identity u . v = ||u|| ||v|| cos(theta). Consequently, non-zero vectors u and v are orthogonal (u perp v) iff u . v = 0, and the signed scalar projection of u onto v != 0 is comp_v(u) = ||u|| cos(theta) = (u . v) / ||v||.

steps: Task: Find k so that u = <4, 6> and v = <3, k> are orthogonal, and compute the scalar projection comp_w(u) of u = <5, 2> onto w = <3, 4>.
For orthogonality, set u . v = 0: 4(3) + 6k = 0 => 12 + 6k = 0 => k = -12/6 = -2.
For u = <5, 2> and w = <3, 4>, compute the dot product u . w = 5(3) + 2(4) = 15 + 8 = 23.
Compute the magnitude ||w|| = sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = 5, so comp_w(u) = (u . w) / ||w|| = 23/5.
workedExample.result: Orthogonal parameter k = -2; scalar projection comp_w(u) = 23/5.

misconception.mistake: Setting components proportional (u_1/v_1 = u_2/v_2) when asked for perpendicular vectors, or dividing by ||v||^2 instead of ||v|| when computing the scalar projection comp_v(u).
misconception.correction: Proportional components (v = c*u) make vectors parallel (collinear), not perpendicular! Perpendicularity requires u . v = u_1 v_1 + u_2 v_2 = 0. And the scalar projection projects onto the unit vector v / ||v||, dividing by ||v|| (whereas the vector projection proj_v(u) = ((u . v)/||v||^2) v divides by ||v||^2 because v itself has length ||v||).

reflection: Notice how the orthogonality test u . v = 0 generalizes negative-reciprocal slopes: if u = <q, p> (slope p/q), then v = <-p, q> (slope -q/p) satisfies u . v = q(-p) + p(q) = 0—and the vector form works even for horizontal and vertical vectors where slope is 0 or undefined!
prerequisiteCheck: Compute the magnitude ||v|| = sqrt(v_1^2 + v_2^2) of the vector v = <5, 12>.
representation: Visualize the right triangle formed by dropping a perpendicular from the tip of u onto the line spanned by v: the shadow length along v is comp_v(u) = (u . v) / ||v||.
